notes.meaning: The priest put the last of the oil on the healed person's head. This was the same oil rite the rich man received. Some teachers note that kings and priests were anointed on the head this way, so it showed great honor to someone who had been an outcast. Matthew Henry sees a picture here: where Christ's blood makes us right with God, his Spirit also makes us holy, and the two always go together. 'Atonement' means making things right between a person and God.

A poor person could bring two doves or two young pigeons instead of two more lambs. One bird was a sin offering, given to deal with sin. The other was a burnt offering, burned whole as a gift of renewed devotion to God. The grain offering came with them. The poor person still went through the very same ceremony as the rich, and was made clean just as fully.

This sums up the special rule for the poor. Being poor did not excuse anyone from bringing an offering. But God asked only what a person could give. The poor were as welcome at God's altar as the rich. Even so, one lamb was still needed, and Matthew Henry sees in it Christ, the Lamb who was slain for us.

God now spoke to both Moses and Aaron about a new matter. Aaron was the high priest, and priests would do the checking. This law was not for the wilderness, where Israel lived in tents. It was for later, when they would live in houses in Canaan.

The law looks ahead to life in the promised land. God says, 'I put' the mildew in a house. The older teachers take this to mean nothing happens apart from God's care and control, whether he sends a trouble directly or allows it. Keil & Delitzsch add that it reminded Israel that their homes, as well as their bodies, belonged to the Lord and should be kept holy.

The owner was to tell the priest at the very first sign of trouble. He did not need to be sure. 'Something like mildew' was enough. Matthew Henry applies this to family life: sin in a home is like a plague, and parents should deal with it early before it spreads.

Before the priest looked, the house was emptied. Things inside became unclean only once the priest declared the house unclean, so clearing it first saved them. This shows the rule was about being fit for worship, not about germs. Wesley sees here that God treats sins done without knowing differently from sins done on purpose.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An older Catholic commentary says the things taken out could be used freely afterward, unless signs of the problem later showed up on clothing.

notes.meaning: The priest looked for greenish or reddish spots that seemed to sink below the wall's surface. These were like the hollow marks on a person's skin with the disease. Keil & Delitzsch compare it to the mold and growths that eat into damp, crumbling walls.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew word for 'depressions' is uncertain. Some translate it 'streaks' or 'eruptions.' 'Wall' here means the plaster surface.

notes.meaning: If the signs were there, the priest stepped outside and shut the house for seven days. This was the same waiting time used for a person with a skin disease. The wait showed whether the problem was real and growing.

After a week the priest came back. If the mildew had spread, the bad stones were pulled out and thrown into the town's dump outside the city. Matthew Henry compares this to cutting off a diseased limb to save the body. In the same way, sin should be removed early before it spreads.

The inside walls were scraped clean, and the scrapings were also dumped outside the city where trash went. New stones and fresh plaster replaced what was taken out. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that people still repair walls damaged by salt deposits in much the same way.
If the mildew came back even after repairs, the priest checked again. If it had spread, it was a 'destructive' mildew that would not go away. Then the whole house was declared unclean.

A house that could not be cleansed was torn down completely: stones, wood, and plaster. All of it was taken to the dump outside the city. Matthew Henry says it was better to have no house than to live in an infected one. He warns that stubborn sin will finally ruin families and churches. He adds that leftover sin stays with us until our bodies, our 'earthly house,' are taken down in death.

While the house was shut up, anyone who went in became unclean until evening. Anyone who slept or ate there had to wash their clothes. These were mild rules that ended by evening. Keil & Delitzsch note that the people were not said to catch the disease. The point was being fit for worship.

If the mildew did not come back after the new plaster, the priest declared the house clean. The problem was gone. This public word set the owner's mind at rest, and his neighbors' too. Matthew Henry notes the house also needed a cleansing ceremony, not just fresh air.

The house was cleansed with the same rite used for a healed person in verses 4-7. The rite used two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop, a small bushy plant. The scarlet may have been a cord tying the hyssop to the wood to make a sprinkler. One bird was killed over fresh, flowing water in a clay pot.

The priest dipped the live bird, the cedar, the hyssop, and the yarn in the blood and water. Then he sprinkled the house seven times. Keil & Delitzsch explain that this cleansed the house from the uncleanness of sin. Sin shows itself first in people, but it reaches the things they touch and live in. Adam Clarke sees a picture of Christ, whose blood must be shed and applied to cleanse a sinner.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular teachers read each item in this kind of rite as a picture of the cross. The cedar is the cross, the scarlet is Jesus' robe, the hyssop is the sponge of vinegar, and the blood and water are from his pierced side.

notes.meaning: Last, the live bird was set free in the open fields. Adam Clarke calls it a 'scape-bird,' like the goat sent away on the Day of Atonement in chapter 16, carrying the uncleanness off. So the priest made atonement for the house, and it was clean. Matthew Henry adds that the house was struck for the owner's sake, and the owner should see himself as spared by God's mercy.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible says the priest 'shall pray for the house' where other versions say 'make atonement.'

notes.meaning: These verses close the long section in chapters 13 and 14. They list all the kinds of trouble covered: skin diseases, mildew in clothes and houses, and swellings, rashes, and spots. Matthew Henry sees God's kind care for his people in these laws. He also sees a call to keep our hearts free from sin and to pray for others to be made clean.

The purpose of the law was to teach when something was clean and when it was unclean. Wesley notes that the priests could not decide by their own will. They had to follow plain rules that ordinary people could also see and understand.
